summary: Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map is a bilingual (EN/UA) web app that turns data from several NASA missions into one interactive model of a future network of autonomous settlements on Mars. In Marswalk mode, an explorer plans a science walk in Jezero crater on layered NASA data (HiRISE, CTX, THEMIS, MOLA/HRSC, CRISM, Mars 2020) and gets a timeline with science stops, daylight and radiation. On the 3D globe, routes are laid on the MGS MOLA elevation grid around steep slopes and hazard zones, and a trip simulator tracks oxygen, water, food, energy and radiation dose using NASA BVAD norms. Five specialised bases (Jezero, Elysium, Arcadia, Utopia, Hellas) exchange water, oxygen, food and energy and are linked by three areostationary relays; the site computes coverage zones, blind spots and failure scenarios such as a relay loss, solar conjunction or a global dust storm. A science guide with 13 articles and 7 NASA missions tags every claim as confirmed, tested by NASA, in development, assumption or calculation. It matters because it helps plan safer Mars missions, supports STEM education and shows how settlements can survive on their own.
details:
What it does

Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map is a bilingual (EN/UA) website that combines data from several NASA missions into one interactive model of a future network of autonomous settlements on Mars. It helps a human explorer plan a Marswalk with science along the way and shows how a group of bases could survive and support each other.

How it works

- Marswalk · Jezero crater: layered NASA data (MRO HiRISE and CTX, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, MGS MOLA / Mars Express HRSC elevation, CRISM/OMEGA hydrated minerals, Perseverance traverse) on one zoomable map. The explorer clicks points, builds a route from the airlock through science stops and gets an EVA plan: timeline, science tasks, daylight and radiation.

- 3D planet: a three.js globe with layers of landing sites, base candidates, minerals, water ice, volcanoes, canyons and dust-storm zones. Routes between regions are found with A* on the MGS MOLA elevation grid and avoid steep slopes and hazard zones.

- Trip simulator: on foot, pressurized rover or hopper; oxygen (based on MOXIE), water (based on ECLSS), food, energy, radiation dose and dust wear along the route, using NASA BVAD life-support values, with markers for hazards, rest stops and the point of no return.

- Network of five bases: Jezero (science), Elysium (energy and spaceport), Arcadia (water and propellant), Utopia (food and manufacturing), Hellas (medicine and radiation shelter). Each base has a life-support page, an autonomy and dust-storm simulator, and exchanges water, oxygen, food and energy with the others.

- Communications: three areostationary relays plus MRO/TGO low orbiters. Coverage zones are computed with MOLA terrain, including overlaps, blind spots and failure scenarios (relay loss, solar conjunction, global dust storm, isolated base).

- Live conditions: Perseverance MEDA and Curiosity REMS weather, Mars season and sun over Jezero.

- Science guide: crew handbook, 13 science articles, 7 NASA missions and quizzes.

Benefits and impact

Mission planners and students can rehearse EVAs and traverses on real NASA terrain and hazard data and test what happens when a relay fails or a dust storm cuts solar power. Teachers get a hands-on STEM tool in two languages. The base network shows how future settlements can share resources and how long each can survive on its own.

Tools and technologies

Next.js 16, React 19, JavaScript (JSX), Tailwind CSS, three.js/WebGL, HTML5 Canvas, A* pathfinding on the MOLA 0.5° grid, NASA Mars Trek tiles and ArcGIS REST services, Mars 2020 MMGIS, MEDA/REMS weather feeds, Vercel hosting, GitHub, and an Android WebView app (Java). No special hardware.

Creativity and factors we considered

Every statement on the site is tagged Confirmed, Tested by NASA, In development, Assumption or Calculation, so NASA facts are never mixed up with our engineering assumptions. We considered radiation limits, communication delay (up to ~22 minutes one way), solar conjunction blackouts, dust storms, terrain slopes, resource consumption rates and offline use (the 3D model works without NASA imagery). Sources come from a registry of 89 NASA pages and peer-reviewed papers based on NASA mission data.
